title: Our experience of time is just as foundational as the physics
subtitle: Time is a model
author: Manuel Delaflor
introduction: We want to trust the clock, dismissing our strange and flexible experience of time as mere "psychological distortion". But philosopher Manuel Delaflor argues this dismissal is a mistake. Drawing on relativity, neuroscience and the strange testimony of anaesthesia and psychedelics, he contends that time is not something that proceeds outside of ourselves, but is generated by minds navigating possibility and constraint. Rather than tracking a hidden reality, Delaflor argues the clock is just one model among many, and a poor one for love, grief, boredom and the moments that change a life.
body:
As I write this piece, I am still discovering where it wants to go, even though it is already written. Wait, what? Is it? No, no, not yet, because I am writing it right now. Then again, that cannot be right, because it is you who are reading it right now. Something is very wrong with the ordinary picture of time.

I am sure you have considered the strangeness of it before the little game above. An hour in a waiting room stretches into something indecent. It thickens. It drags. An hour lost in conversation with a lover disappears before you can even take a breath. The clock on the wall insists that both hours were identical, sixty minutes, three thousand six hundred seconds, a neat little procession of equal units. Your experience insists otherwise, and we simply shrug. “Psychology,” we are told. “Subjective distortion,” we say this as if the clock were stating the actual length, while we are simply wrong. But hold on to that shrug. What exactly is that clock measuring? What gives it the authority to overrule the felt texture of experience?

For most of Western history, time has worn a familiar face: the river. It flows, we are carried, events appear and vanish, childhood recedes, old age approaches.

For most of Western history, time has worn a familiar face: the river. It flows, we are carried, events appear and vanish, childhood recedes, old age approaches. This makes sense. Newton gave this intuition mathematical bones when he described absolute, true, mathematical time as something that flows equably without relation to anything external. There it is, the great cosmic current, the hidden metronome beneath every event. The universe as a billiard table. The balls click and scatter, space holds them, and time passes. The table simply is there. The space it occupies simply extends. Time simply continues, like the river, tick by tick, whether anyone observes it or not. Close your eyes, and the table remains, space holds it, time carries on. This feels so obvious that it barely seems worth saying, which is precisely why it needs to be examined.

Heraclitus gave us the world as flux, the impossibility of stepping into the same river twice. Parmenides stood at the opposite pole, denying change as a trick of mortal minds, insisting that what is, simply is. Augustine perhaps saw the mystery more clearly than either when he asked what time is, and confessed that if no one asks him, he knows, yet if he wants to explain it, he does not. There is the whole problem, naked. Time is perfectly familiar until we try to say what it is. It is the background of every sentence, every memory, every plan, every regret, every promise, yet the moment we turn towards it directly, it seems to dissolve into something unintelligible.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Our future theories of the universe With Roger Penrose, Brian Cox

Science fiction feels this crack and turns it to unexpected places, branching timelines, loops closing on themselves, grandchildren erasing grandfathers, messages causing themselves, interesting ways to travel through it. But travel through what, exactly? Where is “then”? Does the past wait somewhere? Is the future already laid out, merely hidden from our current vantage point? As I see it, these puzzles persist because the concept itself is unstable. Every attempt to pin time down reveals another fracture, another place where the language starts pretending we can understand more than we do.

Then we enter modern physics. Einstein shattered the universal now and the steady, continuous flow. There is no single cosmic present in which everything happens at once. His new idea was that time dilates with speed and gravity. That clocks do not merely measure time from a position outside the problem but participate in the conditions under which temporal measurement becomes possible. This is already devastating for the naive clock. The clock, our little idol of certainty, turns out to show just the small, local, conditional time, obedient to gravity and motion. Then thermodynamics gave us entropy, broken cups that do not reassemble, smoke that does not politely return to the exhaust system. And if we go further, towards quantum gravity, the picture becomes even stranger. In the Wheeler-DeWitt equation, one of the great mathematical symbols of the attempt to bring together the very small and the very large, there is no ordinary time variable doing the work common sense expects from time.

Every attempt to pin time down reveals another fracture, another place where the language starts pretending we can understand more than we do.

So, once again, the questions arise: what exactly are we talking about when we say “time”? A substance? A dimension? A measure? A direction? A relation? And all of this before we have even turned inward, where the problem becomes intimate. Cognitive science has spent decades documenting that temporal experience can be fooled, stretched, compressed, reordered. Chess Stetson and colleagues tested the old claim that fear makes time slow down by dropping participants from a high tower while they watched a device designed to test whether perceptual resolution actually increased. People later judged the fall as lasting longer, but they did not gain the ability to perceive faster information during the fall. This indicates that the dilation was constructed. That detail matters enormously. The feeling that time stretched can be manufactured.

Déjà vu gives us another strange little haunting. The feeling of having been here before arrives without the corresponding past. The unmistakable flavour of already-having-happened, while another part of the system knows this familiarity is inappropriate. This tells us that feeling that something happened before is not a transparent window onto a stored past. It is an operation, a marking, a cognitive achievement. Usually useful, sometimes wrong.

Neurology makes our intuitions feel even more naive. Studies of the right parietal cortex implicate it in temporal judgement and subjective duration. Damage or disruption in the systems that support timing can alter the way succession and interval are organised. Frontal and medial systems are involved in the capacity to project oneself forward, to simulate possible futures, to build the felt reach of what is not yet. Without projection, without the next, without the felt reach of possibility, experience loses one of the tensions that gives time its meaning. The future is the pull through which the present becomes charged with direction. A creature with no anticipation would not experience time as we do. A creature with a different anticipatory structure would inhabit a different temporality altogether or die.

The future is the pull through which the present becomes charged with direction. A creature with no anticipation would not experience time as we do.

At this level, psychoactive substances can stretch, dissolve, or fracture time until language can no longer keep up with its attempts to express it. Eons can pass while “in there.” Entire eons of time. Time can effectively vanish from experience altogether. But at least there is experience left. A different thing happens with anaesthesia: you count backward, the world slips away, and then you open your eyes. The clock says hours have passed, but you were not there for any of it. No slow passage, no fast passage, no waiting, no corridor. Just a before and an after, with nothing in between.

So now the old picture is in real trouble. We began with a waiting room and a lover, with the strange insult of the clock telling us that both hours were identical. We were trained to trust the clock and mistrust experience. Physics has already weakened the idea of a sovereign clock. Cognitive science has weakened the idea of an inner clock. Neurology has weakened the idea that temporal structure is guaranteed. Psychedelics show us that how we feel time can reach heights that are unthinkable, and anesthesia has shown that time can cease completely when experience is gone. At this point, the familiar escape route opens. People will still say, yes, experience is constructed, the brain distorts time, attention stretches it, memory rewrites it, anesthesia interrupts it, but beneath all that, there is still real time, objective time, the physicist’s time, the structure underneath the distortions. Sure, we have not nailed a description, but it is still… there.

You feel it, do you not? The pull to say: yes, fine, all of this is constructed, but somewhere underneath there has to be real time. The physicist’s time, the universe’s own time, the thing the clocks are imperfectly tracking. Notice what you just did. You reached for a foundation. With what? With another model. You demanded a ground that does not depend on any framework, and you demanded it using a framework. Every philosophy that has tried this has run into the same wall. Justify the foundation, and you need another justification, and another, and another, until either the chain runs forever, or it loops back on itself, or you simply stop and pound the table. There is no fourth option.

Let’s pause for a minute (weird thing to say, because of the context) and let me take you to an adjacent road. I have argued elsewhere that what we call objects, colours, sounds, and even the felt boundary of the body are not simply discovered in a pre-given world. They are instantiated by cognitive systems evolved to navigate fields of possibility and constraint. A chair, then, is not just sitting there in metaphysical nudity waiting to be found. “Chair” gathers sittability, obstacle, ownership, memory, design, use, price, context, and action into a workable unity. Colour is not an objective paint laid on surfaces for us to receive correctly. It is a chromatic world generated through language, training, attention, and use. The boundary of the body is not a sacred metaphysical wall. It can be bent by rubber hands, virtual bodies, neurological injury, fear, intimacy. We do not first access reality and then model it. The modelling is the accessing.

SUGGESTED READING Spacetime does not emerge from quantum physics By Sam Baron

Now, if it is already hard to deny for objects, colours, sounds, and selves, the question that has been waiting under this entire essay becomes unavoidable. If objects are constructed rather than discovered, what about the space they supposedly occupy? If events are constructed rather than recorded, what about the time they supposedly occur in? Feel the full weight of this as the inherited picture starts to break. What if space and time are not the stage on which experience unfolds? What if they also belong to the map? Generated by the same cognitive process that generates chairs, colours, bodies, selves, paths, obstacles? What if spatiality emerges with the relations between actionable possibilities and constraints? What if temporality emerges as an orchestration for coordination, anticipation, memory, action? What if we are the ones generating time by weaving what-has-happened into what-can-happen-next, by making fragments navigable, by giving action depth, by allowing error, learning, effort, promise, guilt, grief, expectation to become possible?

Without before and after, there is no story, there is no learning. Without anticipation, there is no risk. Without delay, there is no desire. Without duration, there is no action. Without memory, there is no self. Without future, there is no fear, no hope, no plan, no promise. Time gives rise to a discursive experience, to continuity, and this continuity is not delivered from outside. Past, present, and future are not three cosmic rooms we travel through. This is why the loss of time feels like the loss of self, and why flow feels like self-dissolving into action. This is why boredom thickens it, childhood summers become enormous only after they are gone, and fear can reduce the future to the next few seconds. They are different ways temporality is being made. The Latin root of prediction is praedicere: to say before. Experience is predictive all the way down. It leans forward, prepares, expects, corrects, reaches into possibility and constraint.

We do not encounter time… time is the depth axis […] It is the felt distance between possibility and constraint, the operational cost of a transformation, the pressure of not-yet, the resistance between wanting and reaching.

We do not encounter a chair as a metaphysical object first and then add use to it afterward. We encounter sittability, obstruction, familiarity, context, affordance, and only within that operational field does “chair” stabilize. We do not encounter a cliff as neutral geometry first and then decide it is dangerous but as “do not walk here.” In the same manner, we do not encounter time… time is the depth axis of this same operation that gives rise to chairs and cliffs. It is the felt distance between possibility and constraint, the operational cost of a transformation, the pressure of not-yet, the resistance between wanting and reaching. You can feel this in your own life. If something is easy, it barely registers as temporal. Walking to the table takes a moment. Planning a future, building a career, healing from grief, writing a book, these things take time because they require passage through dense fields of constraint. Difficulty, effort, is what time feels like.

The musician lost in improvisation says three hours disappeared. We call that distortion. The lover says time vanished. We call that altered perception. The grieving person says time stopped. The bored child says time will never end. The mystic says there was only now. Then the clock clears its throat and says: incorrect. But why should it get the final word? The clock is excellent for trains, payroll, surgeries, broadcasts, and satellites, organizing our stuff. But it is disappointingly useless for love, terror, boredom, music, grief, and the intensity of a single moment that changes the direction of a life. The musician in improvisation is not a broken clock. The musician, the hands, the room, the next note, the memory of the last note, the pressure of the phrase, the opening of possibility, all of it becomes one temporal event. The racing driver is not merely “seeing slow motion” compared with the clock in the dugout. The racing driver is inside a temporality where a hundred milliseconds has become rich enough to feel alive.

This is why Model Dependent Ontology matters. It does not ask us to deny the world, worship subjectivity, or pretend that everything is whatever we like, just to stop mistaking our most successful models for access to a model-independent foundation. It tells us that what we call “the world” is instantiated through models that organize possibilities and constraints. Models are tested by what they allow us to do, what they prevent us from doing, what they predict, what they distort, what they make visible, what they erase, what they cost. The clock model works brilliantly for coordination. Relativistic models work brilliantly for satellites. Thermodynamic models work brilliantly for irreversible processes. Cognitive models work brilliantly for lived duration, memory, attention, and anticipation. None of these is telling us “what time is.” Each carves its “isness” through a particular toolkit, without even noticing the carving.

From a Model Dependent Ontology perspective, this is the centre of this essay: What we call past, present, and future are better named context, map, and plan. Context is what has already been gathered, the information that makes action possible at all. The map is the field currently being navigated, the world reorganized around what you are trying to do. The plan is the pull of what has not yet happened, the reach into possibility. These are not three places we travel through. They are three aspects of the single movement by which action becomes possible. Look around and you can feel it. You are thirsty. Instantly, the room stops being scenery and becomes a route. The chair is in the way, the door opens the next step, the kitchen pulls the body forward, the fridge is not an object but a promise waiting behind a handle. Everything you see, touch, and hear has become a map of what is possible and what is not, drawn in relation to the goal. This is what we actually inhabit: not a world of things, but a moving field of possibilities related to specific goals. And the temporal structure of that field is exactly context, map, planning, felt as the shape of acting.

SUGGESTED VIEWING The one and the many With James Ladyman, Sabine Hossenfelder, Ivette Fuentes, Jack Symes

I have been thinking about time all my life. In some ways, I think we all do, like when we see ourselves in the mirror and notice that we are not the same person we used to be. There is violence in that recognition. The face is ours and not ours. The child is gone and not gone. The past has vanished, and yet it can still destroy us, save us, return without permission when a song begins in a supermarket and, suddenly, we are seventeen again, standing somewhere we had not visited in thirty years. When I was seventeen, I wrote something about time. I did not have the vocabulary I have now. I did not have the framework. I did not know how to say models, constraints, temporal structure, operational presence. But I already felt the fracture. I already felt that writing and reading do something strange to time. That the person who writes and the person who reads are not separated in the simple way the clock pretends. That a text is not dead marks from the past. So, I will end with him, because he was already saying in another language what this essay has been trying to say all along:

The time in which I am writing tells my story

I will explain the magnitude of time. Have you noticed how it seems to stop in every thing? Time moves patiently, circling, slipping into every corner and hiding place. It bends and twists to enter through the cracks, and then it expands and fills the emptiness between things. Time can bend and decompose into space. It slowly transforms as we pass. Each breath transforms it a little, and it groans. The other day, I was entering this room, and I saw it moving away. It became small and tried to escape through a crack in the void. So I stopped it, and when I held it, I pressed my fingers into my palm. To hold time, I thought, is to hold my life among the forms.

Now, in another now, always now, I am sitting among the trees. With every movement, I move, but it, it does not move. I am and I am not in this instant, because I lean on my knees and I rest against the bark and I am in the middle of this instant, where the hand of the clock moves without moving. How many versions of me can exist in so many different positions? My astonished mind notices it without believing it, and something inside remains, for eons, without change.

In the suspended instant, I understand that space, and time, and I myself are the same thing. The movement of your eyes confirms it. Right now, as you read, space transforms into this time in which your eyes are running, sliding their gaze across these marks. Did you see it?
